extracted.intended_audience: students, policymakers, and readers of political economy/public finance
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic exposition of principles for designing and assessing taxes (bases, incidence, administration, equity), with historical examples and consequences for rents, profits, and capital. Focuses on which objects to tax (land, houses, stock), how to assess them, and the behavioral and distributive effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish ground-rent vs building-rent
rubrics_metrics.description: What part of the rent ought to be considered as ground-rent, and what part ought to be considered as building-rent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When taxing rents, ascertain and separate the component of rent attributable to the land (ground-rent) from that due to buildings/improvements (building-rent), since tax incidence and fairness may differ between them. The author suggests this distinction 'should not ... seem very difficult.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity / conformity to ability-to-pay
rubrics_metrics.description: The principal objection to taxes upon houses or windows is their inequality; an inequality of the worst kind, as they must frequently fall much heavier upon the poor than upon the rich.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design taxes so they do not disproportionately burden the poor relative to the rich; taxes ought to follow the maxim of proportionality to ability to pay. Beware of objective-but-misleading bases (e.g., window counts) that produce regressive outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative observability and ease of assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Taxes should, where possible, be regulated according to some more obvious circumstance which can be observed without intrusive inspection (e.g., number of windows rather than hearths which required entering rooms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer tax bases that are easy to observe and verify without invasive examinations. The hearth-money required entering every room (odious); the window-tax allowed external counting and was less offensive—illustrating the trade-off between administrative ease and perceived intrusiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade-off: observable proxies vs equity
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrivers of taxes have regulated their taxes according to some more obvious circumstance, such as they had probably imagined would, in most cases, bear some proportion to the rent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using observable proxies (windows, rooms) simplifies assessment but risks inequality and mismatch with actual ability to pay; weigh administrative simplicity against distributive fairness and perverse incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider final incidence (who ultimately pays)
rubrics_metrics.description: A tax upon the profits of stock employed in any particular branch of trade can never fall finally upon the dealers ... but always upon the consumers, who must be obliged to pay in the price of the goods the tax which the dealer advances; and generally with some overcharge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze who bears the ultimate burden: e.g., taxes on merchants/manufacturers tend to be passed to consumers; taxes on farmers generally reduce rent paid to landlords; taxes on stock may be borne by interest or capital owners depending on mobility and substitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid taxing stock/capital directly because of secrecy and mobility
rubrics_metrics.description: The quantity and value of the land which any man possesses, can never be a secret ... But the whole amount of the capital stock which he possesses is almost always a secret ... It is liable, besides, to almost continual variations ... land is a subject which cannot be removed; whereas stock easily may.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct taxation on capital is administratively difficult (secrecy, volatility) and risks capital flight. Prefer bases that are visible and immobile (land) to minimize evasion and emigration of capital; where capital is taxed, expect reduced domestic industry and revenue over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: When assessment is loose/arbitrary, keep tax rates moderate
rubrics_metrics.description: The extreme inequality and uncertainty of a tax assessed in this manner can be compensated only by its extreme moderation; in consequence of which, every man finds himself rated so very much below his real revenue ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If accurate, non-arbitrary assessment of a tax base is impossible, set modest rates to limit unfairness and social friction created by estimation errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid severe inquisitions into private circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: An inquisition into every man’s private circumstances, and an inquisition which, in order to accommodate the tax to them, watched over all the fluctuations of his fortune, would be a source of such continual and endless vexation as no person could support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tax systems should not require constant, intrusive investigations into individuals' private affairs; administrative feasibility and respect for privacy are design constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxes on profits of particular employments shift incidence and distort supply
rubrics_metrics.description: When a tax is imposed upon the profits of stock in a particular branch of trade, the traders are all careful to bring no more goods to market than what they can sell at a price sufficient to reimburse them from advancing the tax ... The price of the goods rises, and the final payment of the tax falls upon the consumer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect supply contraction and price increases when taxing particular trades; the market may supply less, consumers pay more, and some traders may withdraw capital—design taxes to minimize harmful trade-specific distortions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flat licence/fee taxes favour large dealers and can oppress small ones
rubrics_metrics.description: The tax of twenty shillings a-year for a licence to sell ale ... being the same upon all retailers, must necessarily give some advantage to the great, and occasion some oppression to the small dealers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid uniform flat charges across heterogeneous-sized businesses if the policy goal is to preserve competition; proportional or scale-sensitive charges reduce bias toward concentration and monopolization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxes on agriculture (personal taille) discourage cultivation and reduce productivity
rubrics_metrics.description: In the countries where the personal taille takes place, the farmer is commonly assessed in proportion to the stock which he appears to employ ... he endeavours to cultivate with the meanest and most wretched instruments ... he probably loses more by the diminution of his produce, than he saves by that of his tax.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tax schemes that target agricultural capital or use visible but manipulative measures lead to underinvestment, degraded cultivation, and long-term harm to production and national wealth; design agricultural taxation carefully to avoid perverse incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poll-taxes have different implications on slaves vs freemen
rubrics_metrics.description: What are called poll-taxes ... upon every negro, are properly taxes upon the profits of a certain species of stock employed in agriculture ... A poll tax upon slaves is altogether different from a poll-tax upon freemen. The latter is either altogether arbitrary, or altogether unequal, and, in most cases, is both the one and the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that poll taxes on enslaved persons function as taxes on capital stock and are administratively straightforward for masters, whereas poll taxes on freemen are often arbitrary and regressive; normative and ethical differences must inform tax design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-assessment/source-of-truth requires social trust
rubrics_metrics.description: At Hamburg every man assesses himself, and, in the presence of the magistrate, puts annually into the public coffer a certain sum of money, which he declares upon oath ... This tax is generally supposed to be paid with great fidelity. In a small republic, where the people have entire confidence in their magistrates ... such conscientious and voluntary payment may sometimes be expected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-assessment regimes can work where civic trust, small population, and confidence in use of revenue exist; don't rely on voluntary declarations in large, distrustful polities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxes on servants and similar per-head levies function like consumption taxes
rubrics_metrics.description: The taxes which in Holland are imposed upon men and maid servants, are taxes, not upon stock, but upon expense ... The tax of a guinea a-head for every man-servant, which has lately been imposed in Great Britain, is of the same kind. It falls heaviest upon the middling rank.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify per-person servant taxes as taxes on consumption/expense and anticipate distributional effects (middling classes hit hardest); use classification to predict incidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxes on transfers reduce capital value; use stamp duties/registration to tax secret movable property
rubrics_metrics.description: While property remains in the possession of the same person ... permanent taxes ... never intended to diminish any part of its capital value; But when property changes hands ... such taxes have frequently been imposed upon it as necessarily take away some part of its capital value. The transference of stock or moveable property ... is frequently a secret transaction ... It has been taxed indirectly ... by requiring that the deed ... should be written upon paper or parchment which had paid a certain stamp duty ... or that it should be recorded ... and by imposing certain duties upon such registration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the aim is to tax transfers (which necessarily affect capital), use instruments like stamp duties and mandatory registration to reach otherwise hidden movable transactions; accept that transfer taxes reduce capital values and are distinct from taxes on ongoing revenue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider market demand and elasticities when predicting tax effects on rents/prices
rubrics_metrics.description: The natural tendency of the window tax, and of all other taxes upon houses, is to lower rents. ... Since the imposition of the window tax, however, the rents of houses have, upon the whole, risen ... Such has been ... the increase of the demand for houses, that it has raised the rents more than the window tax could sink them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume mechanical effects; evaluate demand-side conditions and elasticities—taxes that would lower rents in one environment may be offset or reversed by strong demand, affecting policy outcomes.
